title: Identifying grapes
subtitle: Fingerprints of the classics
objectives: Recognise the main white grapes blind
Recognise the main red grapes blind
Use structure as much as aroma

steps.title: White fingerprints
steps.body: Sauvignon Blanc: pronounced grass, gooseberry, high acidity, no oak. Riesling: lime, flowers, high acidity, sometimes sugar and petrol. Chardonnay: neutral fruit shaped by place and oak, often butter and toast. Gewürztraminer: lychee, rose, low acidity, high alcohol. Chenin Blanc: apple, quince, honey, high acidity.

steps.title: Red fingerprints
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon: blackcurrant, cedar, high tannin. Merlot: plum, softer tannin. Pinot Noir: pale, red fruit, low tannin. Syrah: blackberry, pepper, deep colour. Nebbiolo: pale but very tannic, rose and tar. Sangiovese: sour cherry, high acidity, tea-like tannin. Structure often reveals more than aroma.
steps.highlight: Tannin and acidity reveal the grape

steps.prompt: Match each wine description to its grape.

pairs.left: Sour cherry, high acidity, tea tannin

steps.explanation: Combining aroma and structure gives the clearest identification.

steps.title: Common confusions
steps.body: Some grapes are easily confused. Pinot Noir and Gamay are both pale and red-fruited; Gamay is often juicier, with banana notes from carbonic maceration. Cabernet and Merlot blend so often it's hard to separate them. Albariño and Grüner Veltliner both show citrus and acidity; Grüner adds white pepper.

steps.prompt: A wine that is pale in colour must be low in tannin.
steps.explanation: Not true. Nebbiolo is pale but very tannic, a classic blind tasting trap.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Each white grape has an aroma plus acidity fingerprint
Red grapes are often identified by tannin and acidity
Know the common confusions, like Pinot Noir and Gamay
